strengths: Clearly defines and motivates the NLQ4TSDB task, and convincingly differentiates it from Text-to-SQL (expressivity bottleneck) and end-to-end TSQA (context-length bottleneck), framing the two-sided challenge well.

Introduces NLQTSBench with a sensible four-level taxonomy (basic ops, pattern recognition, semantic reasoning, insight synthesis) and tailored metrics (IoU, set-F1, composite report score), which is a genuinely useful resource for the community.

The Search-Then-Verify pipeline is a coherent, training-free engineering solution: SAX/statistical feature tables for high-recall symbolic search, then LLM-generated Python operators for exact verification on raw data. Prompts, operator library, and construction pipeline are documented, supporting reproducibility.

The ablation study is informative and internally consistent: removing Verify causes the largest collapse (Avg 0.62→0.25), and removing Feature Tables specifically damages morphology tasks (CT 0.30→0.04), supporting the claimed division of labor.
The case study on 'longest plateau' concretely illustrates why pure SQL and pure TS models fail and how search-then-verify succeeds, grounding the abstract claims with evidence.
Honest about one limitation (SAX compression loses fine local detail in short windows) and reports the counterintuitive finding that training-free MAC-SQL beats fine-tuned SOTA SQL models.
weaknesses: The benchmark is authored, and the proposed method is evaluated on it with the authors' own metrics, producing uniformly dominant results. There are no independently curated or task-adapted baselines and no third-party validation, so the headline gains are hard to separate from benchmark design choices.

No variance, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported; all results appear to be single runs. LLM nondeterminism (DeepSeek-V3 planner/generator, self-correction retries) is not characterized, weakening the reliability of the reported deltas.

Baseline comparisons are of questionable fairness: Text-to-SQL methods are run off-domain (they lack morphological primitives by design), and time series models are artificially restricted to cropped 512-point windows, so their low scores partly reflect the setup rather than intrinsic capability. This supports the paradigm argument but not a strong 'we beat SOTA' claim.

Scale claims are overstated relative to the artifact. The abstract appeals to TSDBs with 'millions of points,' yet NLQTSBench is 831 queries over ~170k points with query windows averaging ~11k points; 'large-scale' and 'massive' are used loosely, and Level 2 windows are only ~0.6k points.

Component-level novelty is limited: SAX indexing, LLM-generated SQL+Python, runtime self-correction, and the Reward-Summarize-Update experience loop (adapted from training-free GRPO) are all pre-existing; the contribution is primarily combinatorial and application-driven rather than a new mechanism.

The benchmark is built from a single source dataset (CausalRivers) with synthetic injection for Levels 2–4. Although labeled 'auditable by construction,' injected-and-labeled patterns may not capture real-world morphological ambiguity; the human verification is described but lacks annotator count, inter-annotator agreement, and rejection rates.

Reproducibility and practical cost are under-reported: no latency, token/compute cost, index-build time, or storage overhead for the multi-scale feature tables, which are central to the efficiency claims. There is no explicit limitations section, and the reference list contains errors (Pelkonen cited as 2023 but listed as 2015; duplicate 'Pourreza et al. (2023)' for both DIN-SQL and CHASE-SQL).

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely interesting and under-explored problem: natural language querying over TSDB-scale histories where the intent is morphological rather than purely relational. Framing this as distinct from both Text-to-SQL and short-context TSQA (Section 1, 2) is a reasonable conceptual contribution.

The 'Search-Then-Verify' pipeline (Section 4.3.1) is an intuitive and sensible design: coarse SQL-based pruning over a symbolic index (SAX feature tables) followed by Python verification on raw signals. The sonar analogy is well-motivated and the modular architecture (offline indexing / online querying / post-processing) is coherently described.

The ablation study (Table 2) is informative: removing verification collapses performance (0.62 -> 0.25), and removing the feature tables severely degrades morphology tasks (CT 0.30 -> 0.04), which supports the central design claim that symbolic search plus algorithmic verification is necessary.

The benchmark taxonomy (Levels 1-4) is thoughtfully structured (Section 3.1, Figure 2) and the data construction pipeline attempts to balance realism (real CausalRivers backgrounds) with auditable ground truth via controlled injection and human verification (Section 3.2, Appendix A.2).
weaknesses: The benchmark's realism and the fairness of the evaluation are the central problems. Ground truth for Levels 2-4 is produced by injecting synthetic parametric primitives (Gaussian spikes, dual-sigmoid boxes, sinusoids) onto real backgrounds, and queries are generated from a small set of templates (Appendix A.2.2). The system is therefore evaluated largely on recovering injected, templated artifacts rather than genuine open-ended user intent, which undercuts the paper's claim of measuring real NLQ4TSDB capability.

Calling NLQTSBench 'the first large-scale benchmark' (Abstract, Section 3.3) is overstated. 831 queries is small by Text-to-SQL standards (Spider ~10k, BIRD ~12k), and the L2/L4 subsets are 80-100 items each, which is too small to support strong statistical claims.

Several reported scores are implausibly high given the difficulty framing (Table 1): Subsequence Matching IoU of 0.9535 and Periodicity Detection of 0.8529 are near-ceiling on tasks the paper claims are hard. This raises concerns about evaluation leakage, loose metric tolerance (e.g., permissive IoU for injected intervals), or an over-easy benchmark, none of which is investigated.

The baselines are not appropriately adapted to the task. MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL, and Omini-SQL are general relational Text-to-SQL systems with no morphological primitives, so their failure on shape tasks (SI, CT) is expected rather than informative. Critically, there is no strong in-domain baseline such as an LLM agent that directly generates Python to scan/slice the raw series (or an SQL+Python agent without the feature index). The ablation 'w/o Feature Tables' (Table 2, avg 0.6168 -> 0.5572) actually suggests the proposed symbolic index contributes only modestly on average, which is never confronted as a baseline question.

There is no statistical rigor: no multiple runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite the framework relying on an LLM (DeepSeek-V3) with stochastic self-correction and a learned 'Experiences' memory. Reported differences (e.g., 0.6168 vs 0.5572) cannot be judged reliable without variance estimates.

The novelty is largely engineering recombination: SAX indexing (Lin et al., 2007), LLM task planning/code generation, retry-based self-correction, and an experience-summarization memory (Cai et al., 2025). The 'Prompt Cold Start' Reward-Summarize-Update loop is a standard prompting/experience-accumulation technique applied here, and no mechanism is analytically justified over simpler alternatives.

Reproducibility is limited: the backbone is a proprietary LLM (DeepSeek-V3), the feature-table and operator library details are only partially specified, and the full benchmark (queries + executable evaluation programs) is not clearly released (only NLQTSBench-Lite is promised). This makes it difficult for others to verify or build on the results.

Presentation and reporting issues reduce confidence: inconsistent/incomplete metric description (Level 4 composite score is oddly numbered '4.0.4' with hand-tuned weights w1=0.4, w2=0.3, w3=0.2, w4=0.1 with no sensitivity analysis), Table 2 claims 'cells highlighted in blue' that are not visible, and typos ('scalars' -> 'calars'). No human evaluation is provided for the Level 4 report-generation task despite its importance.

The qualitative claims outrun the evidence: the Abstract/Conclusion assert Sonar-TS 'effectively navigates complex temporal queries where traditional methods fail,' but the only supporting evidence is a comparison against unadapted baselines on a self-constructed synthetic benchmark, with low absolute morphology scores (SI 0.3169, CT 0.3033).

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a genuinely useful and under-explored problem: natural language querying over TSDB-scale histories with morphological intents. The distinction from Text-to-SQL and short-context TSQA is clearly motivated and practically relevant.

NLQTSBench is a substantial contribution: 831 queries across a four-level taxonomy, long histories (~170k points, ~11k-point query windows on average), a Lite variant for context-limited TS models, and deterministic metrics for scalars, intervals, sets, and structured reports.

The benchmark construction pipeline is relatively careful: it combines real background series (CausalRivers) with controlled injection, distribution-aware parameter sampling, SNR/ambiguity checks, and human visual verification. This improves auditability over purely synthetic or manually annotated data.

The Sonar-TS framework is a sensible and well-engineered neuro-symbolic pipeline: offline multi-scale feature tables with statistical primitives and SAX signatures, LLM-based task planning, hybrid SQL+Python generation, a domain-specific verification operator library, runtime self-correction, and experience summarization. It is training-free and practical.

The experimental results are promising on the proposed benchmark: Sonar-TS outperforms Text-to-SQL methods on the full benchmark and time series models on NLQTSBench-Lite. The ablation study isolates important components, especially verification (avg. 0.62 -> 0.25 when removed).

The appendix provides useful implementation detail: SAX/PAA formulation, operator signatures, prompt templates, experience-update prompts, and metric definitions. This materially improves reproducibility relative to a high-level system description.

The paper is generally well written and the figures effectively communicate the Search-Then-Verify workflow and the benchmark taxonomy. The Impact Statement appropriately flags privacy and access-control risks for sensitive industrial deployments.
weaknesses: The external comparison is not fully convincing. Text-to-SQL baselines are evaluated as pure SQL generators, while Sonar-TS receives a feature index, a Python execution environment, and a curated operator library. A fairer baseline would be an LLM code agent with raw-data access, SQL, and Python (but no Sonar-TS index/operators), or Text-to-SQL methods augmented with the same tools. Without this, the claim that traditional methods 'fail' may partly reflect unequal tool access rather than a fundamental paradigm gap.

The benchmark and method appear co-designed: the benchmark task subtypes align closely with Sonar-TS's verification operators (ACF for periodicity, DTW for subsequence matching, PELT for segmentation, Theil-Sen for trend slope, Pearson for causal correlation). This risks favoring the proposed method, and the paper does not analyze or control for this alignment.

There is no statistical rigor over LLM stochasticity. Results appear to be single-run, with no seeds, confidence intervals, variance across runs, or sensitivity to backbone model, prompt templates, temperature, or retry budget. Since Sonar-TS is training-free and LLM-driven, this is a material reproducibility and reliability concern.

The claimed scale is overstated. The benchmark contains ~170k points globally and 831 queries, while the introduction motivates the task with TSDBs containing 'millions of points.' The empirical setting is much smaller than the motivating scenario, and no latency, memory, or cost analysis is provided for large histories.

The SAX-based symbolic index is coarse, and the paper itself notes information loss in short windows. However, there is no sensitivity analysis over SAX alphabet size, window lengths, phase offsets, normalization, or alternative tokenization methods, despite the framework's claim to be tokenization-agnostic.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section. It does not discuss failure modes, prompt brittleness, SQL dialect/generalization beyond InfluxDB-like systems, dependence on injected patterns, human-verification reliability, metric design choices, or ethical/data-license constraints for the benchmark.

Evaluation metrics need more justification. The Level-4 composite report score uses manually chosen weights (0.4/0.3/0.2/0.1) that are described as calibrated but not validated. The timestamp hit-rate tolerance of zero may be overly strict or brittle depending on timestamp representation.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: there is no clear code/data release link, no explicit train/test/validation split, no random seeds, and no specification of how many human annotators participated or how disagreements were resolved during visual verification.

Several presentation and reference issues remain, e.g., CHASE-SQL is listed under a 'Pourreza et al. (2023)' label despite being a 2025 ICLR paper, and 'Omini-SQL' is used inconsistently. These are minor but suggest insufficient proofreading.

The time series model baselines are evaluated only on NLQTSBench-Lite, while Sonar-TS is evaluated on both Lite and full. Although this is justified by context limits, it prevents a direct end-to-end comparison and weakens the claim that Sonar-TS handles the full task better than time series models under identical conditions.

strengths: The paper clearly defines a new task (NLQ4TSDB) with a formal problem formulation (Eq. 1–2) and articulates three concrete challenges (representation gap, context-scale limit, semantic grounding conflict) that are well motivated and distinguish the setting from Text-to-SQL and TSQA.

NLQTSBench is described with a genuinely documented construction pipeline: parameterized templates with constrained semantic slots, parametric primitive injection (Gaussian, dual-sigmoid, sinusoid) with SNR calibration (1.0 < SNR < 1.5), variance-based background rejection, and human visual verification (Fig. 6). This is more rigorous than typical synthetic benchmarks, and the four-level taxonomy is sensible.

Sonar-TS is a coherent, well-engineered system: multi-scale offline feature tables with SAX tokens as a symbolic search handle, an LLM task planner that explicitly chooses between DIRECT_ACCESS and SEARCH_THEN_VERIFY, a hybrid SQL+Python generator with a bounded self-correction loop, and an operator library grounded in established algorithms (PELT, DTW, Theil–Sen, ACF, Pearson).
The offline 'Reward–Summarize–Update' experience distillation avoids fine-tuning and online memory updates, and is built on a held-out 110-query set, which is a reasonable way to avoid test leakage.

The empirical section includes an informative ablation (Table 5) that identifies qualitatively different failure modes, parameter sensitivity over LLM backbone and SAX alphabet size (Tables 8–9), internal search-stage recall (Table 10), overhead analysis (Table 11), and a qualitative case study (Fig. 5).
The limitations appendix (Appendix D) is honest about synthetic data, SAX information loss, and the non-scalable static experience set, and the impact statement is appropriately cautious.
weaknesses: The benchmark scale directly contradicts the paper's central motivation. Table 2 reports an average search space of ~12k points (L3 ~30k), not the 'millions of points' repeatedly invoked to justify the architecture. At 12k–30k points, a brute-force Python scan or simple chunking is trivially feasible, so the necessity of the symbolic index is not demonstrated; the offline construction time (~83 s) and storage overhead (11%) in Table 11 also suggest a small underlying dataset. The claim that this magnitude 'enforces a paradigm shift' is unsupported.

There is a strong circularity/leakage concern between benchmark construction and the proposed system. Ground truths are generated from parametric primitives (Gaussian spikes, dual-sigmoid plateaus, composite sinusoids, injected correlation breaks), while Sonar-TS's verification operators (detect_changepoints, calc_trend_slope, detect_period, find_best_MATCH, calc_correlation) are essentially matched to those same primitives. The verification stage is therefore aligned with the generative model of the labels, and the reported numbers likely overestimate real-world generalization. This is not discussed.

The baseline comparison is not apples-to-apples. Text-to-SQL and TS models are given neither the feature index nor the operator library, so their failure is partly by construction. The 'w/o Feature Tables' ablation—a generic SQL+Python agent—already reaches 0.5430 average versus 0.6144 for the full system, indicating that most of the headline gap over baselines comes from the agentic SQL+Python pipeline rather than from the symbolic index. A brute-force scan baseline and a retrieval-augmented agent with the same operator library but no index are missing.

No variance, error bars, or multiple runs are reported, despite the pipeline being stochastic (LLM planning, code generation, self-correction). Differences such as w/o Self-Correction (0.5930) vs. full (0.6144) are within plausible run-to-run noise and should not be interpreted as they are.

The search-stage recall is only 0.47–0.55 (Table 10), and one of the injected experiences (Fig. 4) explicitly instructs the system to fall back to fetching the entire raw range when SAX filtering returns nothing. The frequency and impact of this fallback are never reported, yet they directly determine whether 'Search-Then-Verify' actually performs search or degenerates into full scanning.

The Level 4 evaluation uses a hand-weighted composite (0.4/0.3/0.2/0.1) whose weights are asserted to be 'calibrated' without any validation, and the deterministic parsing relies on a prompt-enforced vocabulary/schema that may inflate scores relative to open-ended report generation. Level 1's relative-accuracy metric is also easy, and it inflates the reported average.

Several framing claims are overstated relative to the evidence: 'first large-scale benchmark' when per-query scale is ~12k points; 'effectively navigates complex temporal queries where traditional methods fail' when the failures are partly engineered by baseline configuration; and the abstract's dangling 'Our code has been made available at' with no visible artifact in the reviewed version.

The work is largely an integration of known components (SAX indexing, LLM code generation, standard TS operators, experience distillation) applied to a newly coined task; the conceptual originality of 'Search-Then-Verify' is modest and closely resembles standard candidate-generation-then-verification pipelines in IR/databases. There is also limited evidence that this is a machine-learning contribution of interest to the ICML audience as opposed to a systems/database engineering contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and under-explored problem: natural language querying over time series databases, clearly distinguishing it from Text-to-SQL and TSQA.
NLQTSBench introduces a structured four-level taxonomy covering a wide range of query types, from basic numerical retrieval to morphological pattern recognition and insight synthesis.
The Sonar-TS framework is well-motivated and modular, combining symbolic indexing (SAX) for efficient candidate search with Python-based algorithmic verification.
The appendix provides extensive implementation details, including prompt templates, operator library, and benchmark construction pipeline, which aids transparency.
The ablation study systematically analyzes the contribution of each component, showing that feature tables, experiences, and verification are all important for performance.
The paper includes an honest limitations section discussing synthetic data, SAX information loss, and experience scalability.
weaknesses: The benchmark scale does not match the claimed problem scale: the paper motivates NLQ4TSDB with 'millions of points' and 'ultra-long histories', but the benchmark's average search space is only ~12k points. This fails to test the scalability challenge (C2) that is central to the paper's motivation.

No fair baseline for the core claim: Sonar-TS is compared only to Text-to-SQL methods (which generate SQL only) and time series models evaluated on short 512-point windows. A generic LLM agent that generates Python to scan raw data (feasible at 12k points) is not compared, so the advantage of symbolic search over brute-force verification is not demonstrated.

The time series models fail even on short contexts (NLQTSBench-Lite), undermining the paper's claim that context length is the primary bottleneck. The results suggest morphological and logical reasoning are the main challenges, not scale.
Performance on the core morphological tasks is low: Shape Identification achieves 0.3336 IoU and Composite Trend 0.2988 F1, indicating the method does not effectively solve the central challenges.
The SAX-based search has low recall (0.5482 for SI, 0.4713 for CT), severely limiting the system's upper bound. The paper acknowledges this but offers no solution.

The benchmark is entirely template-based and synthetic, with ground truth injected. The 'Experiences' are distilled from a hold-out set of 110 queries likely using the same templates, risking overfitting. No evaluation on real or differently generated queries is provided.
The Level 4 evaluation metrics use arbitrary weights (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1) without validation, and the parsing success rate of the LLM's free-form output is not reported.
Reproducibility issues: no URL for the promised code, lack of details on human verification (annotator agreement, rejection rate), and no description of the experience initialization dataset.

The novelty is limited: the framework combines existing components (SAX, Text-to-SQL, LLM code generation, retrieve-then-verify) in a pipeline. The 'Experiences' mechanism is essentially prompt memory with hand-crafted heuristics.

The comparison to Text-to-SQL baselines is potentially unfair because Sonar-TS has access to precomputed feature tables and Python execution, while baselines are only given SQL generation. It is unclear whether baselines could access feature tables or execute Python.
System latency (~22s per query) is high for interactive use, and the paper does not discuss incremental updates or scalability to many channels.
The paper overstates the benchmark as 'first large-scale benchmark' when 1,153 queries is not large-scale, and the synthetic nature limits its realism.

strengths: The paper clearly formulates a new and practically motivated task, NLQ4TSDB, and sharply distinguishes it from Text-to-SQL and TSQA through the MP/MS/NLG capability analysis (Table 1), which usefully frames the problem space.

It introduces the first benchmark for this setting, NLQTSBench, with a well-organized four-level taxonomy (basic operations, pattern recognition, semantic reasoning, insight synthesis) plus a short-context Lite variant, and documents query templates, construction pipeline, and metrics in the appendix.

The Sonar-TS framework is a sensible and well-motivated neuro-symbolic design: a multi-scale SAX feature index for SQL-based candidate search followed by operator-based Python verification, with an offline experience/cold-start mechanism. The execution-complexity analysis (Eq. 3) correctly argues decoupling from series length N.

The empirical study is broad and informative: main comparisons, component ablations with qualitatively distinct failure modes, backbone sensitivity, SAX alphabet sensitivity, an internal search-stage evaluation, and a system-overhead comparison against MAC-SQL.

The limitations discussion (Appendix D) is honest and specific about synthetic injection, SAX information loss, and the non-scalable static experience injection, and the code/operator library is released.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the benchmark: queries are instantiated from templates and the ground truth is the synthetically injected pattern (Section 4.2, Appendix A.2), i.e., exactly the structure the SAX search + verification machinery is built to recover. This makes it hard to conclude that the reported gains reflect real-world NLQ4TSDB capability rather than alignment between the benchmark and the proposed method. This is acknowledged but not resolved.

The baseline comparison is uneven. Text-to-SQL baselines (MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL, Omni-SQL) are not given feature tables or Python verification, so the large gaps on morphology tasks partly reflect the added tooling rather than the design of Sonar-TS. A stronger comparison would adapt a baseline into a comparable SQL+Python agent (as the 'w/o Feature Tables'/'w/o Verification' ablations effectively do) and report it as a baseline.

Absolute performance on the core morphology tasks remains low (SI 0.33, CT 0.30), and the internal search-stage recall is only ~0.47–0.55 (Table 10), which upper-bounds the whole pipeline. The claim that Sonar-TS 'effectively navigates' these queries is stronger than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility/credibility issues: the backbone models are listed as 'Qwen3.5-9B/27B/35B' (Table 8), which do not correspond to known model releases, casting doubt on the sensitivity analysis; the composite report score weights in Eq. 12 are 'calibrated' with no reported procedure or validation.

No variance, error bars, or statistical significance are reported anywhere despite LLM stochasticity and multi-step agentic execution, so it is unclear whether the reported differences (e.g., in ablations) are stable.

Metric design is not validated: the controlled-vocabulary, two-part report schema may inflate Level-4 scores, and several metric choices (relative accuracy for scalars, IoU for intervals) are adopted without sensitivity analysis or human correlation.
